title: On The Price of Freedom
author: Antonius Veritas
summary: This Stoic Manual essay pairs Buck, the pampered dog of Jack London's The Call of the Wild, with Epictetus's teaching on freedom. Just as Buck becomes unshakable once hardship strips away his dependence on comfort, Epictetus argued that anyone who needs external circumstances to cooperate is not truly free. The piece recounts Epictetus's example of a freed slave who immediately enslaves himself again to patrons, office, and possessions. Its central claim is that whoever can give you what you think you cannot do without, or inflict pain you believe you cannot endure, is your master. The author clarifies that the goal is not withdrawal from work or relationships but inner detachment from outcomes, and closes with a Discourses passage and a set of Socratic self-examination questions.
points: Buck's transformation in the Klondike illustrates how circumstances lose power over someone who learns to endure deprivation.
Epictetus's freed slave shows how people trade one form of servitude for new dependencies on wealth, status, and possessions.
Needing approval, a client, or a reputation hands leverage to anyone who can withhold or damage those things.
The prescribed practice is to engage fully in work and relationships while leaving outcomes to the universe and locating one's good in character and choices.
quotes: Buck picks himself up and transforms into a pillar of endurance. Circumstances lose their power over him as he traverses beyond the limits of what he thought possible.
He himself was enslaved- but he argued that a person needing the cooperation of external circumstances to go on about life was no free man.
Anyone who can’t endure embarrassment, loss, criticism or exclusion gives people who can inflict these dangers leverage over them.
This is why he often concluded that, Your master is the person who can give you what you think you can’t do without, or one who can inflict pain you believe you can’t endure.
Needing another person’s opinion or approval will dictate your mood. Needing a client to stay makes their departure terrifying.

A person is free when they can live as they choose: when they cannot be compelled, obstructed, or forced into what they wish to avoid. Whoever places their good in things controlled by others has made themselves dependent on them.
